description: Hey! We are Vistronix from Qarshi. We love digging into data and building cool stuff with AI and code. For the "Earth System Trend Detective" challenge, we want to turn raw NASA satellite data into a story everyone can actually understand and feel. You don't need to be a rocket scientist to join us if you are curious about Earth science, love coding, data viz or just crafting great stories, let's team up and build something awesome together.
summary: STAND-IN is a coverage planner, not another ranking of "Moon-like" places. Instead of asking which Earth site looks most like the Moon or Mars, it asks which requirements of a test campaign a place can actually cover — and how far the data behind that answer can be trusted. We cross nine Earth candidate sites, from Iceland to the dried Aral Sea bed, with twelve test requirements. Every cell is marked covered, partial, insufficient data or not applicable, together with its evidence. Using NASA elevation, laser-altimetry and imagery data plus ESA and JAXA datasets, we found that one Aral seabed transect returns a single elevation value (31.0 m) at all 481 points over about 133 km: a property of the map, not of the ground. Result: 3 requirements can be covered by a place, 4 partly, and 5 only by artificial facilities.
details:
The problem. Analog sites are usually chosen by name and appearance. Two questions are rarely made explicit: which specific test requirement can a place cover, and is the map data we use to say so reliable at all?

What STAND-IN does. We define twelve test requirements for a lunar or Martian base analog. For nine Earth candidates, plus Mars (Jezero) and Moon (Shackleton, Mons Malapert) reference targets, we compute a coverage table. Each cell is covered, partial, insufficient_data or not_applicable, with a confidence value and a stated reason. A separate "evidence status" per site says whether the data can support the requirement at all.

How it works. A reproducible Python pipeline reads open datasets through STAC catalogs and cloud-optimised GeoTIFFs (windowed reads, no bulk downloads): NASADEM, Copernicus GLO-30 and ALOS AW3D30 elevation; JRC Global Surface Water history; MODIS vegetation index; NASA POWER temperatures; MRO CTX and Kaguya terrain models; LRO LOLA laser altimetry; and NASA GIBS imagery (MODIS true colour; HLS 30 m for the candidate sites). Slope is recomputed on a common local 100 m grid. DEMs are never subtracted from each other, because their vertical datums differ. A noise floor for each source is derived from its documented vertical error, so differences smaller than the floor are not ranked. An automated verification script checks every published number against pipeline outputs. The website is static and works offline. Live site: https://stand-in-eqs.pages.dev

What we found.

(1) Aral Sea bed. NASADEM returns one value, 31.0 m, at all 481 points of a transect about 133 km long; Copernicus GLO-30 is also constant in a 20 km window. A nearby dry control shows 140 distinct values (std 49.31 m). In a 20 km window of the same area, JRC records surface water in 79.1 % (v1.4) to 83.8 % (v1.3) of observations. We call this a possible historical-water artifact: NASADEM's source mask is unavailable, so we cannot separate water flattening from void filling.

(2) Ranking is not supported. Expressed as slope, documented vertical errors set noise floors of 9.09° (NASADEM), 2.29° (Copernicus) and 1.72° (CTX). Many candidate differences fall below them.

(3) Mars (Jezero). At one point, 22 overlapping CTX terrain models disagree by a median of 54.9 m; 40 % of sample points have at least one empty model. Our code reproduces three published USGS values.

(4) Moon (Shackleton). For the same point the Kaguya catalog lists 109 items, 75 real raster footprints, and none holds a valid pixel at the target. A sunlit control site run with the same code works. We make no claim about the cause.

(5) Coverage. Three requirements are coverable by a place, four partly, and five (gravity, vacuum, radiation, regolith mechanics, rover-scale hazard) only by artificial facilities.

Limits. STAND-IN audits data sources; it is not a field assessment. NASADEM and ALOS are not fully independent of each other. The noise floor is a conservative bound, not a confidence interval. We changed two choices after seeing results, and we disclose both: the vegetation summary (from the maximum to the 95th percentile, because the maximum depends on sample size), which moved both Ustyurt candidates from partial to covered; and the measurement area (from a 20 km transect to a 5 × 5 km window, so each row describes one area), which moved Haughton's dry-surface cell from covered to partial. Both old and new values are kept. The vegetation threshold (95th-percentile NDVI below 0.2 counts as vegetation-free) is our own choice: NASA's documentation gives no value between 0.1 and 0.2, so every vegetation cell is marked low-confidence. EMIT mineral data were not used. We report Haughton (Earth) and Shackleton (Moon) both near 7° median slope as an interesting coincidence, not a validation.

Tools. Python (rasterio, GDAL, NumPy, SciPy, laspy, shapely), HTML/CSS/JavaScript.

Use of AI. The team developed the project through discussion and made all final decisions. AI assistants were used as thinking partners, to draft code and text, and an AI design tool to explore the layout; the team questioned, reviewed and corrected their output. All data come from the cited public sources; every published number is computed by scripts and checked automatically. No images were generated by AI.
